extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and students of poetics/literature
extracted.subtask_description: Norms and evaluative criteria for composing poetry (especially epic and tragedy): diction, metaphor, metre, plot-unity, use of episodes, plausibility, and treatment of errors. Targets poets, playwrights, and critics assessing poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of strange/rare words and propriety
rubrics_metrics.description: A diction that is made up of strange (or rare) terms is a jargon; a style wholly composed of such words is either a riddle or a jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infuse an authorial style with some strange or rare words, metaphors, and lengthening/ornamental forms to raise it above the commonplace, but avoid making the whole style unusual. Example anti-patterns: prose entirely of metaphors (riddle) or entirely of rare words (jargon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metaphor as the chief quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor; this alone cannot be imparted by another; it is the mark of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor shows an eye for resemblances and is the most powerful device for distinction. Cultivate ability to ‘make good metaphors’; it is the most important stylistic gift and not reducible to mere technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate employment of lengthening, contraction, alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing contributes more to produce a clearness of diction that is remote from commonness than the lengthening, contraction, and alteration of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deviate in exceptional cases from normal idiom to gain distinction, but retain partial conformity with usage so that perspicuity remains. Critics who censure these licenses are mistaken; obtrusive use is grotesque (Eucleides’ parody).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obtrusive or ludicrous license
rubrics_metrics.description: To employ such license at all obtrusively is, no doubt, grotesque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rare words or odd forms used without propriety and with the express purpose of being ludicrous produce a grotesque effect. Use unusual diction only where it fits tone and aim; examples given (parodies) show the anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching word-kinds to poetic species
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the various kinds of words, the compound best adapts to dithyrambs, rare words to heroic poetry, metaphors to iambic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the kinds of diction according to genre: dithyrambs favour compounds and double names; heroic (epic) accepts rare words and metaphors; iambic suits metaphorical usage. In verse imitating familiar speech, prefer current/proper words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of an infusion, not entire composition, of ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain infusion, therefore, of these elements is necessary to style; ... while the use of proper words will make it perspicuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure a measured mixture: ornamental and metaphorical elements should raise style while proper/current terms maintain clarity. Too much ornament obscures meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (single plot with beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot manifestly ought, as in a tragedy, to be constructed on dramatic principles. It should have for its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build narrative imitation (even in single metre forms) around one coherent action so the work resembles a single organism and produces its proper pleasure. Avoid composing a poem of many unrelated episodes that do not conduce to a single result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish narrative subject from historical composition
rubrics_metrics.description: It will thus resemble a single and coherent organism, and produce the pleasure proper to it. It will differ in structure from historical compositions, which of necessity present not a single action, but a single period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat a poem like a chronicle of simultaneous but unrelated events (e.g., separate battles occurring together). Keep poetic plot focused on action rather than merely listing occurrences within a period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of episodes in moderation and to diversify
rubrics_metrics.description: He detaches a single portion, and admits as episodes many events from the general story of the war—such as the Catalogue of the ships and others—thus diversifying the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes may be admitted to vary the poem and relieve monotony, but they should not undermine the unity of the central action; in tragedy, episodes must be limited by stage representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale/length must allow apprehension of beginning and end
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view. This condition will be satisfied by poems on a smaller scale than the old epics, and answering in length to the group of tragedies presented at a single sitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set a practical upper bound on scope so the audience/hearer can grasp the whole. Epic may be larger than tragedy but should not be so vast as to lose unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic’s special capacity for enlarging dimensions via narration
rubrics_metrics.description: In Tragedy we cannot imitate several lines of actions carried on at one and the same time; we must confine ourselves to the action on the stage. But in Epic, owing to the narrative, there can be many parts simultaneously made to take effect, and these, if relevant to the subject, add mass and dignity to the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrative mode to include simultaneous or distant actions that contribute to grandeur; this is an advantage of epic over stage-bound tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of metre—heroic for large narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all measures the heroic is the stateliest and the most massive; and hence it most readily admits rare words and metaphors ... no one has ever composed a poem on a great scale in any other than heroic verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metre that fits the subject and scale: heroic metre for lofty narrative and large scale; iambic and trochaic tetrameter for action and stirring/choral effect. Avoid mixing metres (Chaeremon’s error).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature teaches the choice of proper measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature herself, as we have said, teaches the choice of the proper measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the character of the imitation (stateliness, action, dance-like quality) determine meter rather than arbitrary preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit authorial intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak—as little as possible in his own person, for it is not this that makes him an 'imitator.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize direct authorial voice; let characters and imitation carry the work. Homer praised for bringing in characters with minimal prefatory authorial comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope for the wonderful and the irrational
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the wonderful is admitted in Tragedy. The irrational, on which the wonderful depends for its chief effects, has wider scope in Epic poetry, because there the person acting is not seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use marvels/irrational incidents where medium conceals action (epic narration) or where plausible; on-stage depiction of absurdity may become ludicrous. The wonderful pleases and can be used to charm the audience when handled skillfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inventing departures from reality, make them plausible relative to the story-world (a falsehood that leads the mind to infer a true antecedent) rather than merely shocking or incredible events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude irrational elements from the action when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: The irrational should, if possible, be excluded; or, at all events, it should lie outside the action of the play ... not within the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the plot requires irrational incidents, place them outside the dramatic action (narrated or otherwise framed) or make them credible by giving them an air of likelihood; otherwise they make the plot ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction elaboration only in pauses
rubrics_metrics.description: The diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action, where there is no expression of character or thought. ... character and thought are merely obscured by a diction that is over brilliant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornate or highly polished diction for moments between actions; avoid dazzling language when conveying character or thought, where clarity is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of poetic faults: essential vs accidental
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the art of poetry itself there are two kinds of faults,—those which touch its essence, and those which are accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the fault arises from inability to imitate what was chosen (intrinsic), it is more serious; if from mistaken choice about incidental matters (accidental), it is less so. Critics should distinguish these when evaluating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors may be justified by the end of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: If a poet has described the impossible, he is guilty of an error; but the error may be justified, if the end of the art be thereby attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An otherwise 'erroneous' element is acceptable when it produces a stronger poetic effect (e.g., more striking pursuit scene). But if the same end could be achieved without violating poetic rules, the error is unjustified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take account of speaker/actor/context in judging poetic rightness
rubrics_metrics.description: In examining whether what has been said or done by some one is poetically right or not, we must not look merely to the particular act or saying, and ask whether it is poetically good or bad. We must also consider by whom it is said or done, to whom, when, in whose interest, or for what end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate utterances and deeds in light of character, occasion, audience, and purpose (e.g., to secure a greater good or avert a greater evil). Context can change whether something is poetically proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solve critical difficulties by choices among representation modes and language
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet, being an imitator, must of necessity imitate one of three objects—things as they were or are, things as they are said or thought-to be, or things as they ought to be. The vehicle of expression is language—either current terms or, it may be, rare words or metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When resolving ambiguous or problematic passages, consider whether the poet is representing reality, belief, or norm; use accent, punctuation, ambiguity of construction, or usage/idiom to interpret lines. Examples: accent/breathing, punctuation, ambiguity (πλέω), or dialectal usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language usage and dialect may legitimately alter meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes an expression is metaphorical or dialectal (e.g., 'all' used for 'many', specific local word-usage changing sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sensitive to regional usages, metaphors, and conventional polysemy when composing or interpreting lines; rare words may be intended in non-literal senses (examples: οὐρῆας, εὐειδές, ζωρότερον).
